online_ai_brief.summary: The best zero-budget route is to build one small product once, publish the free core on GitHub Releases or a static page, and sell the upgrade through a storefront that settles stablecoin to the already-validated Tron address; Getly is the strongest current fit because the lead describes free listing, no monthly fee, and USDT/USDC payout to the seller's own wallet with no KYC for crypto settlement, while the wallet ask and GitHub Releases remain the zero-platform fallback. Skip Sellix entirely: it was seized in 2024. Chrome Web Store is the only channel with a real one-time cost, so use it only for an extension and only if the owner accepts $5 once; otherwise stay on GitHub, Getly, itch.io with KYC caveat, and the existing dev.to articles.

market_themes.theme: Free distribution does the discovery; monetization happens beside the product, not inside the store.
market_themes.evidence: Chrome Web Store, GitHub Releases, itch.io and dev.to are free or near-free places to publish; the wallet ask and Getly are the ways the free audience converts to money.
market_themes.offer: Ship the useful core free where users already search, then sell a one-time upgrade, preset pack, or licence from the README, product page, and article footer.

market_themes.theme: Direct stablecoin settlement to an own wallet is the rare no-custodian path; fiat storefronts usually pay the price of identity checks.
market_themes.evidence: Getly is described as paying USDT/USDC to the seller's own wallet with no KYC for crypto settlement; itch.io requires a tax interview, TIN, and a one-time Tax Identity fee.
market_themes.offer: Use Getly as the paid channel and keep the raw TRC-20 address as the no-platform fallback; treat itch.io as optional only if fiat payout and tax disclosure are acceptable.

market_themes.theme: The same artifact can be listed on many zero-cost channels without multiplying work.
market_themes.evidence: The local playbook explicitly recommends listing one product on every free channel, and this project already publishes dev.to articles with a validated receive address.
market_themes.offer: Build once, then point GitHub Releases, the product page, the README, the article footer, and one storefront listing at the same download and the same upgrade.

market_themes.theme: An unenforced ask travels with every copy, while enforcement lives only at the purchase point.
market_themes.evidence: GitHub Releases, FUNDING.yml, README, --help output, and docs footers can all carry the same address; the local playbook found that a receive path attached only at publish time missed most readers.
market_themes.offer: Put the address in the README and inside the tool itself, not only on the listing page, so users who never open the storefront can still pay.

refused_channels.name: Sellix
refused_channels.why: Seized and shut down in 2024. Still widely recommended as the crypto storefront, which is exactly why it is written down here as refused.

refused_channels.name: Gumroad (for crypto)
refused_channels.why: Does not natively accept crypto and pays out USD via Stripe only. Fine as a fiat storefront; it is not a crypto receive path, and mrr_ideas should not imply it is.

refused_channels.name: Buy Me a Coffee / Ko-fi (main platforms)
refused_channels.why: No native stablecoin field for a supporter's own wallet. Ko-fi Web3 is a separate product on BEP-20 only, so the wallet footer already covers this better.

refused_channels.name: Any custodial crypto payment processor
refused_channels.why: Holds the money before the owner does. The published Tron address is non-custodial and already works; adding a custodian adds KYC risk for no gain.

refused_channels.name: Coinbase Commerce
refused_channels.why: DEFUNCT. Permanently shut down 2026-03-31 for merchants outside the US/Singapore, with no extensions offered. Its replacement (Coinbase Business) is fully custodial and US/Singapore only. Still recommended in current listicles -- a Sellix-class trap.

refused_channels.name: CoinPayments
refused_channels.why: Geo-dead and KYC-mandatory. EU/EEA service discontinued after 2026-07-01 under MiCA, and the current platform requires identity verification for all users, not just above a threshold.

refused_channels.name: kofi.network
refused_channels.why: IMPOSTOR RISK -- not affiliated with ko-fi.com despite the name and a '(c) 2026 Ko-fi' footer. No operator disclosure. It advertises wallet-to-wallet USDT on BEP-20, which is exactly the property that would rank it highly here, which is why it is written down as refused rather than left to be rediscovered.

refused_channels.name: NOWPayments (as a direct channel)
refused_channels.why: Marketed as non-custodial, but the default flow routes funds through their wallet and KYC triggers at volume and always for fiat. Reached indirectly anyway: it is the rail Getly uses to dispatch payouts, so using it directly adds a custodian without adding a storefront.

refused_channels.name: Gitcoin / Allo
refused_channels.why: Wound down. Grants Lab and Grants Stack reached end-of-life 2025-05-31 and Allo is in maintenance mode. KYC applies above $15k matching regardless.

refused_channels.name: Drips Network
refused_channels.why: Genuinely non-custodial and plausibly identity-free, but Ethereum ERC-20 only. It cannot reach the Tron address this project publishes, so it would need a second address and a second meter (Principle 3f) to earn a cent.

refused_channels.name: BTCPay Server
refused_channels.why: The only fully non-custodial, fee-free, no-KYC option on the table -- and it needs a server. This project has none (GitHub Actions is outbound-only), and third-party hosting reintroduces the dependency it exists to avoid. Refused on infrastructure, not on merit.

refused_channels.name: Gumroad, Substack, Polar, GitHub Sponsors, Ko-fi, Buy Me a Coffee, Payhip, Liberapay, Lemon Squeezy, Paddle, Open Collective
refused_channels.why: All require identity verification, directly or through Stripe/PayPal onboarding, and none settles crypto to a seller-controlled address. Verified 2026-09-15 after the owner hit exactly this wall on Gumroad and Substack. Buy Me a Coffee is the specific trap: it accepts crypto from buyers but converts to USD and pays out via Stripe, US accounts only.

constraints: Runs on GitHub Actions free tier: hourly, outbound-only, no always-on server.
No inbound HTTP. Nothing can accept a request, a form, or a webhook.
No payment processing. Nothing can charge a card or bill a subscription.
No outreach. Cold email, DMs, and social posting are refused in code.
Can research, analyse, draft, and publish articles to dev.to. That is the whole surface.
mrr_ideas.summary: The single best angle is a deeply niched paid newsletter for a developer sub-niche the owner can genuinely research — for example, GitHub Actions cost and reliability engineering — where every issue is drafted by the automation, edited and published by the owner to dev.to as free previews that build the byline audience. Because the stack has no payment processor and no outreach, money can only arrive passively-but-honestly: the owner publishes a personal wallet address (Tron) for voluntary subscriptions/tips, which needs no account, no ID check, and no storefront, and later — only if the audience justifies it — opens a Gumroad account by hand and passes its ID verification to sell subscriptions at a fixed price. Nothing here is autopilot: the owner must hand-write the buyer-facing parts, answer comments, and keep the wallet address visible on every article.

ranked_ideas.name: Paid newsletter (GitHub Actions cost & reliability digest)
ranked_ideas.why_this_stack_fits: The stack's entire surface — research, analyse, draft, publish to dev.to — is exactly what a written digest needs; no server, no inbound HTTP, and hourly GitHub Actions runs fit the workflow.
ranked_ideas.narrow_niche: Teams and solo maintainers whose GitHub Actions bills are climbing — specifically digest of Actions workflow cost traps, flaky-cache issues, and runner misconfigurations, with a worked fix per issue.
ranked_ideas.first_proof_artifact: A 3-part free series on dev.to: 'Auditing your GitHub Actions bill by hand' — one issue per week, each ending with an invitation to subscribe via the published wallet address, plus the raw checklist as the first paid deliverable.
ranked_ideas.who_pays: Maintainers of mid-size open-source repos and indie devs self-hosting CI who are personally responsible for the Actions bill.
ranked_ideas.runway_to_first_dollar: 6-12 weeks (byline audience must exist first; verify independently any income expectation)
ranked_ideas.owner_must_do_by_hand: Publish each issue to dev.to themselves (no auto-posting trust built yet), reply to comments, keep the wallet address in the byline/footer, and manually record who paid via wallet transfers — no automated subscriber management exists in this stack. Later, if volume justifies it: open Gumroad by hand

ranked_ideas.name: Notion / digital template store (Actions-cost audit template)
ranked_ideas.why_this_stack_fits: The draft capability can produce the template's content and its dev.to launch article; the store itself is one static product, not a service, so no inbound HTTP is needed after setup.
ranked_ideas.narrow_niche: A single Notion template: 'GitHub Actions spend-audit workbook' — per-workflow cost worksheet, redundancy checklist, and a monthly re-audit ritual.
ranked_ideas.first_proof_artifact: The free checklist from the newsletter series turned into the actual Notion workbook, plus a dev.to article walking through one real (anonymised) audit using it.
ranked_ideas.who_pays: The same reader as the newsletter: a repo maintainer doing their first spend audit who wants the structure done for them.
ranked_ideas.runway_to_first_dollar: 8-16 weeks (requires the newsletter articles to have built readership first; verify independently)
ranked_ideas.owner_must_do_by_hand: Build the Notion workbook manually, open a Gumroad account by hand and pass its ID verification before any fixed-price sale, or publish the wallet address and honour tips manually. Fulfilment (sending the template link) is done by hand per buyer.

validation_steps: Write a dev.to article that audits a real-looking Actions bill step by step and ends with a direct question: 'What does your monthly Actions bill look like, and which workflow scares you? Reply in the comments.' — comments are inbound, permitted, and tell you who has the problem.

Manually check dev.to comment threads, Reddit CI threads, and GitHub community discussions for people complaining about Actions costs; note who they are and what they ask — this is research, not outreach. Log 10 distinct people-with-the-problem observed, verify independently.

Ask, in a hand-posted comment or reply inside communities the owner already participates in, whether a $10/mo digest plus a $15 template would be worth it — framed as a question about their needs, not a pitch.
Watch wallet tips and dev.to follower growth for 4 weeks: if nobody tips or engages after 8+ published articles, the niche or price is wrong — iterate before building the Gumroad store.
